subject: health
unitTitle: Mental Health Maintenance and Sustainable Coping
title: Guided practice: sleep, isolation, and workload as leading indicators
focus: sleep, isolation, and workload as leading indicators
essentialQuestion: How do I keep myself steady through a transition that removes most of my structure?
keyPoints: Changes in sleep, isolation, workload, concentration, or daily functioning can serve as early signals to adjust load and seek support without self-labeling.
Match the response to the level of need: use a practical coping step for ordinary strain, add trusted support when functioning is disrupted, and use urgent help for immediate danger.

For sleep, isolation, and workload as leading indicators, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Write a transition plan with maintenance strategies, early-warning conditions the learner will watch for, and a concrete first step for getting professional support — including how it would be paid for and accessed.
studentTask: Complete a fictional support-plan card for sleep, isolation, and workload as leading indicators: identify one observable signal, choose one immediate coping or communication step, name a routine support route and an urgent route, and explain why the plan does not make a peer responsible for care.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in sleep, isolation, and workload as leading indicators; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
